content: The International Grape Genomics Program (IGGP) is a collaborative initiative aimed at sequencing the genome of the grapevine species Vitis vinifera L.. This multinational project involves research centers from Australia, France, Chile, Germany, Italy, South Africa, Spain, and the United States. The program was established based on the understanding that, despite the economic importance of the Vitis family as a source of fruit, its biology remains poorly understood. Although viticulture has been practiced for centuries, providing a wealth of knowledge in wine production, the precise mechanisms by which grapevines interact with their physical environment, respond to abiotic stresses, and combat pests and diseases are not yet fully elucidated. Historically, agricultural practices for Vitis have relied on specific genotypes, with improvements in quality and yield achieved through vegetative propagation and controlled growing conditions. However, these advancements have come at increased costs and potential environmental sustainability challenges. The IGGP posits that a deeper understanding of the biology of Vitis could lead to significant improvements in viticulture without the associated ongoing costs. By sequencing the grapevine genome, researchers aim to identify the roles of individual genes in viticulture, enabling predictable enhancements in grape characteristics and quality. As of March 2007, the IGGP had successfully mapped over half of the grapevine genome. During their research, the Cooperative Research Centre for Viticulture (CRCV) in Adelaide, Australia, discovered that white grapes exist today due to a rare genetic mutation that occurred thousands of years ago. This mutation involved two adjacent regulatory genes, VvMYBA1 and VvMYBA2, in a red grape ancestor. These genes control the presence of anthocyanin, the pigment responsible for red coloration in grape skins. In white grapes, the VvMYBA1 gene is not transcribed, and the VvMYBA2 gene is rendered inactive by two mutations: one causing an amino acid substitution and the other a frameshift mutation. Either mutation alone disrupts the gene's ability to activate anthocyanin biosynthesis, and when both are present, the result is a white grape cultivar. Sequence analyses confirmed that all 55 white grape cultivars tested shared the same double mutation in the VvMYBA2 gene, indicating a single common ancestor. This suggests that without this original parent vine, white grapes would not exist today. Residues of white wine found in ancient Egyptian pottery suggest that this mutation occurred at least 3,000 years ago. However, without direct testing against a known white grape genome, it remains possible that the mutation arose more recently. Interestingly, a similar dual mutation was observed in the last decade. In Rioja, Spain, viticulturist Jesús Galilea Esteban identified a white grape mutation in some Tempranillo vines on his estate. The first hectare of white Tempranillo was planted in the region in 2000. Both white and red Tempranillo vines share identical leaves, clusters, and berry shapes, as well as the short ripening cycles and susceptibility to pests and diseases typical of red Tempranillo. The mutation is believed to have been triggered by environmental factors.
